title: Brew Line With No Waiting
statement:
A potion shop has n brewers standing in a line and m potions to make, in the given order. Every potion passes through brewer 0, then brewer 1, and so on to brewer n − 1.

Brewer i spends skill[i] × mana[j] time units on potion j. A brewer works on one potion at a time.

The mixture is unstable: the moment a brewer finishes a potion, the next brewer must take it immediately. A potion can never wait between brewers, so you may have to delay when a potion starts at brewer 0. Potions start in order, and potion j + 1 starts no earlier than needed.

Return the time at which the last brewer finishes the last potion, starting at time 0.

examples.why: Potion 0 runs 0–2 at brewer 0 and 2–8 at brewer 1. Potion 1 must reach brewer 1 no earlier than 8, so it starts at 7: 7–8, then 8–11.
Brewer 0 is free at 3, but starting potion 1 then would reach the slow brewer 2 at 5 while it is busy until 21. It must start at 19, finishing at 19 + 1 + 1 + 5 = 26.
With a single brewer the potions just run back to back: 6 + 2 + 8.

hints: For one potion, everything is fixed once you choose its start time t: it reaches brewer i at t + (skill[0] + … + skill[i − 1]) × mana[j].
Remember when each brewer finishes the previous potion. Every brewer gives a lower bound on t; take the largest.
Equivalent two-pass trick: push the potion forward as early as each brewer allows, then walk backward from the last brewer to recompute the finish times with no gaps.

explain.intuition:
Because a potion never waits, its whole schedule is one rigid block that slides in time. If it starts at t, it reaches brewer i at t + pre[i] × mana[j], where pre[i] is the total skill of the brewers before i. The only question is how early the block can slide.

Brewer i is busy until done[i], the moment it finished the previous potion. So t ≥ done[i] − pre[i] × mana[j] for every brewer. The smallest valid start is the largest of these bounds. Then update every done[i] to t + pre[i + 1] × mana[j] and move on. Starting each potion as early as possible never hurts later potions, because every brewer is then free as early as possible too.
steps: Compute pre[i], the prefix sums of skill, and set done[i] = 0 for all brewers.
For each potion with mana x: t = max over i of done[i] − pre[i] × x.
Set done[i] = t + pre[i + 1] × x for every brewer.
pitfalls: Starting each potion when brewer 0 is free. The second example shows a slow brewer further down forcing a later start.
Letting the potion wait in front of a busy brewer. That breaks the rule and gives an answer that is too small.
Only comparing with the last brewer. Any brewer can be the bottleneck, depending on how mana changes between potions.

solutions.title: Bump the start until nothing clashes
solutions.idea: Try to start the potion when brewer 0 is free. Walk the line; at the first busy brewer, delay the start by exactly the clash and walk again from the top.

solutions.title: Largest lower bound on the start
solutions.idea: Each brewer i forces start ≥ done[i] − pre[i] × mana. Take the maximum, then rewrite every brewer's finish time.

followups: With n and m up to 100 000 the O(n · m) loop is too slow. The bound is a maximum of linear functions in x. Which geometry trick answers it fast?
What if potions may be reordered freely?
